title: From Pixar to the Top of the World: Taylor Swift’s Record-Breaking Week
summary: What do you get when you mix a beloved Pixar franchise with one of the biggest pop stars on the planet? A global chart-topper, apparently. Taylor Swift’s “I Knew It, I Knew You,” from the upcoming Toy Story 5, rocketed to No. 1 on the Billboard Global 200 this week, pulling in a staggering 51.5 million streams and 91,000 downloads worldwide in its first seven days. That’s a monumental debut—and it makes Swift the solo artist with the most No. 1s in the chart’s history, with seven. Only BTS, with eight leaders, has more among all acts. The song is also a landmark for animated films: it’s only the second Global 200 No. 1 from a Disney animated feature, and the first from Pixar. The previous Disney chart-topper was the ensemble earworm “We Don’t Talk About Bruno” from Encanto in 2022. On the U.S.-based Billboard Hot 100, Swift added her 15th career leader with this track, joining an elite club of Disney themes that includes “A Whole New World” from Aladdin back in 1993. The song’s success isn’t just about numbers—it’s a cultural moment. Swift performed it live for the first time at the Toy Story 5 Hollywood premiere on June 9, and the film opens wide on June 19. The Global 200 chart, which ranks songs based on streams and sales from over 200 territories, reflects a truly worldwide embrace. Meanwhile, Ariana Grande’s “Hate That I Made You Love Me” slipped to No. 2, and Drake’s “Janice STFU” fell to No. 3. On the Global Excl. U.S. chart, which excludes American data, Swift’s song debuted at No. 3, while Grande held at No. 1. Swift’s trajectory on the Global 200 is remarkable: from “All Too Well (Taylor’s Version)” in 2021 to this latest triumph, she’s consistently turned personal storytelling into global phenomena. With Toy Story 5 poised to be a summer blockbuster, “I Knew It, I Knew You” is likely just getting started.
why_it_matters: This story shows how music can break records when a superstar artist and a beloved movie franchise combine forces — and it hints that the ways people around the world consume music are more connected than ever, shaping what you might hear in your own playlists.

background_read: The Billboard Global 200 (a weekly music chart launched in September 2020) ranks songs based on streaming and digital sales data from more than 200 countries and territories, giving a true picture of a song's worldwide popularity.
BTS (the South Korean supergroup that became one of the best-selling acts globally, with fans on every continent) has earned eight Global 200 No. 1s, more than any other artist.

The 2022 Disney film Encanto (set in Colombia, with songs by Lin‑Manuel Miranda) spawned the viral hit "We Don’t Talk About Bruno," which topped charts around the world without a traditional music video.

Pixar (the innovative computer‑animation studio behind Toy Story, founded in 1986 and later owned by Disney) has released beloved films that often produce iconic songs, but only this track has become a Global 200 leader for the studio.

The Billboard Hot 100, which covers only U.S. data, has been the standard popularity gauge since 1958; "A Whole New World" from Aladdin reached No. 1 there in 1993, making it a rare animated‑film chart‑topper.

perspectives.description: Taylor Swift cements her status as a global solo icon by extending her record, while Pixar and Disney gain a rare chart-topping hit that can drive movie ticket sales and deepen emotional ties with audiences.

Some may worry that a tie-in song for a major franchise pushes out independent or smaller artists from the top of the charts, and that chart dominance by a few superstars makes the music industry feel less diverse.

The Global 200, which blends data from over 200 territories, shows that a song can become a worldwide phenomenon by tapping into both streaming culture and nostalgia for familiar animated worlds — a pattern seen before with "Encanto" and likely to repeat.

As the Toy Story 5 movie opens, the song’s success may grow even further, but the real question is whether Swift can sustain this momentum over the summer and whether other artists will try similar soundtrack partnerships to capture global audiences.
